rashi:a1.1: No sanctity takes effect upon them: This applies even to the middle [case], where they are the offspring of consecrated animals: even the sanctity of their mother does not take effect upon them, since it says “no sanctity” without qualification.
rashi:a1.2: As they come into being: When they are born; and therefore no sanctity at all takes effect upon them.
rashi:a1.3: But the sanctity of their mother has taken hold of them: From the moment its formation began, each and every bit is sanctified.
rashi:a1.4: Rather, learn from it: The whole mishna is [according to] Rabban Shimon [ben Gamliel].
tosafot:a1.1:
In brief: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds they are sanctified as they come into being; therefore no sanctity takes effect on a tumtum or a hermaphrodite, since before the mother’s sanctity could reach them they were already blemished, and his own words do not sanctify them either, as he does not intend blemished animals. Had he held they are sanctified in the womb, the mother’s sanctity would have reached them while they were not yet blemished, since the case is a consecrated animal.

Question: perhaps his reason is that one who consecrates intends only a definite male or a definite female (Bava Batra 140b)? Answer: then they would still receive the mother’s sanctity, yet he says no sanctity at all takes effect.

Question: Rav Ḥisda (Bekhorot 41b) says all agree a tumtum is an uncertain case and sanctity takes effect out of uncertainty. Answer: for Rav Ḥisda, “no sanctity” means sanctity by his words, since he intends only a definite male or female; and the Gemara’s argument here does not follow Rav Ḥisda.

Question: if they are like blemished animals, why does Nidda 40b need a verse that if they were brought up on the altar they are brought down? So too Zevaḥim 112a–114a needs “before the Tabernacle of the Lord” to exempt one who offers such animals (including offspring of consecrated animals) outside, implying they would otherwise be fit for “the entrance of the Tent of Meeting”. And by the Ri’s explanation in Bava Kamma 77b (“or a goat” excludes a nidmeh among offspring of consecrated animals), kilayim, which are worse (Bava Kamma 78a), are surely unfit; why exclude them again?

Answer: those animals are indeed not sanctified at all, yet the verses are needed, since while still in the womb they could come before the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, or into the courtyard, with their consecrated mother, though they themselves are not sanctified.

gershom:a1.1: He holds they are sanctified as they come into being: At the time they are born, and at that time they are already recognizable as a tumtum or a hermaphrodite, and they are not sanctified. For if it enters your mind that they are sanctified while still in their mother’s womb, etc.
rashi:a2.1: If it were not stated, etc.: This refers to this verse (Leviticus 27:26): “But the firstborn which is born as a firstling to the Lord among animals, man shall not consecrate it.”
rashi:a2.2: If it were stated: The firstborn which is born as a firstling shall not consecrate: And “man … it” were not written, and “among animals” were not written, I would have said that a firstborn man may not consecrate anything at all to the Temple.
rashi:a2.3: The verse states “it”: Since it says “it”, this implies that it speaks of a firstborn animal too, and this is what it means: But a firstborn man, who is born as a firstling, shall not consecrate it, the firstborn animal. It he does not consecrate: a firstborn man may not consecrate a firstborn animal, but he may consecrate other consecrated items. And “among animals” is still not needed [for this], and it comes for this exposition, as we say: One might think that he, a firstborn man, may not consecrate it, a firstborn animal, but others, other people who are not firstborns, may consecrate a firstborn animal with a different sanctity.
gershom:a2.1: And this that he said, that they are sanctified as they come into being, comes to exclude this tanna, as it is taught: If it were stated “But the firstborn shall not consecrate” — this verse that is written, “But the firstborn which is born as a firstling,” etc. That is, if it were stated “But the firstborn which is born as a firstling to the Lord among animals shall not consecrate,” and “man … it” were not stated, I would have said the verse implies that a firstborn man may not consecrate consecrated items, as I would have said that “But the firstborn which is born as a firstling to the Lord” is a firstborn man, who shall not consecrate at all. Therefore it states “shall not consecrate it”: a firstborn animal one shall not consecrate, as it already stands consecrated, but one may consecrate other animal consecrations.
rashi:a3.1: The verse states “among animals”: Which was not needed [for the earlier exposition], and [it comes] to reveal about the verse that it does not speak of a firstborn man.
rashi:a3.2: I am dealing with animals: I spoke here of a firstborn animal, that no person may consecrate it with a different sanctity, and I did not speak here of a firstborn man at all.
gershom:a3.1: And still I say: A firstborn man [may not] consecrate a consecrated item, and not an ordinary [man]. [The wording is terse; the sense is that the restriction might apply only to a firstborn man.]
gershom:a4.1: Among animals: I am dealing with a firstborn animal and not with a man. That is, the verse [says “among animals”] because it does not speak of a firstborn man but of a firstborn animal; but a man may consecrate consecrated items, whether he is a firstborn or an ordinary man.
rashi:a4.1: In the womb: That even while it is still in the womb one cannot consecrate it with a different sanctity.
rashi:a4.2: From the time it is born as a firstling: From the time it is sanctified at the opening of the womb; but in the womb it is non-sacred.
gershom:a5.1: One might have thought not: That one would not be permitted to consecrate the firstborn with a different sanctity even when it is still in its mother’s womb.
gershom:a6.1: The verse states: “Which is born as a firstling to the Lord”: That is, you may not consecrate it once it is born, but you may consecrate it in its mother’s womb with a different sanctity. One might have thought that even the offspring of all consecrated animals one could consecrate in their mothers’ womb, to change them from their mothers’ sanctity, like a firstborn fetus.
rashi:a5.1: One might have thought that even the offspring of all consecrated animals are so: That it is permitted to change it to a different sanctity while it is still in the womb.
rashi:a5.2: The verse states: “But the firstborn”: “But” distinguishes: with a firstborn I permitted you to consecrate it before it is born as a firstling, but not other consecrated animals in the womb. For since its mother is consecrated, each and every bit that is formed in it is seized by the sanctity, as the offspring of consecrated animals are sanctified in their mother’s womb. And he does not hold like the tanna of our mishna.
gershom:a7.1: The verse states: “But”: It excludes. Evidently he holds that the offspring of consecrated animals are sanctified in their mother’s womb and are seized by their mother’s sanctity; or perhaps a firstborn is different.
rashi:a6.1: He said with regard to the firstborn: While it is still in the womb: at the emergence of its majority, when the sanctity of a firstborn is due to take effect upon it, at that moment let the sanctity of a burnt offering take effect upon it, and not before. So now there are two sanctities coming to take effect together: which of them is more stringent and takes effect first, pushing aside the other?
rashi:a6.2: Is it a burnt offering: As it is entirely consumed.
rashi:a6.3: Or is it a firstborn: As the sanctity of the firstborn takes effect on all the firstborns in the world from the womb.
tosafot:a6.1: He said with regard to the firstborn: At the emergence of its majority it will be a burnt offering: Specifically at the emergence of its majority. But had he said at the emergence of its minority, there would be no dilemma, as the burnt offering certainly takes effect on it, since the sanctity of a firstborn has not yet taken effect on it at all.
gershom:a8.1: Each and every bit that exits: Remains in its matter, in the essential sanctity of the firstborn itself.
gershom:a9.1: Another version: Is it a burnt offering, since it is a stringent sanctity and takes effect upon it; or perhaps it is a firstborn, since it is sanctified from the womb, which is not so with other consecrated animals, and it is stringent.
rashi:a9.1: When the majority falls: When it is due to become gleanings.
rashi:a9.2: Will be ownerless: Even for the wealthy. Which of them takes effect upon it? For it is certainly clear to us that had he declared all the grain ownerless before this, it would not be obligated in gleanings, since only that which is food and guarded is obligated.
gershom:a10.1: He said with regard to gleanings: Regarding the stalks of gleanings, at the time when most of them fall to the ground, for the essential law of gleanings is that which falls to the ground; and he said: Let it be ownerless.
gershom:a11.1: Is it gleanings, as it is sanctified by the hand of Heaven, Who commanded that it be gleanings; or perhaps it is ownerless, as its force is greater, since both poor and wealthy acquire it.
rashi:a11.1: And Abaye said: What is his dilemma? Certainly, since they come to take effect together — the words of the Master and the words of the student — certainly the words of the Master take precedence, and the Holy One, Blessed be He, made it gleanings.
rashi:a11.2: So too, the words: Of the Master take precedence here as well, and it is a firstborn.
gershom:a12.1: And Abaye said: The words of the Master take precedence: [It is] the decree of Heaven, and it is gleanings. Here too, with a firstborn, the words of the Master take precedence, and it is a firstborn.
rashi:a12.1: MISHNA: One who says: With regard to the offspring of a pregnant animal.
rashi:a12.2: Its offspring is a burnt offering and it is a peace offering, his statement stands: For the sanctity of the offspring came first.
rashi:a12.3: But if he said: It is a peace offering: First, for the mother, he consecrated it and all that is in it, and the offspring is considered as consecrated in its own right, and it is like one who consecrates two animals as peace offerings; and when he then said “its offspring is a burnt offering,” the offspring is a peace offering. And here it is not relevant to say “as they come into being” or “in their mother’s womb.” For when we say “as they come into being” and not in their mother’s womb, that applies where he consecrated it and afterward it became pregnant, where he did not involve the fetus in any sanctity and it is sanctified only through the sanctity of its mother; but where one consecrates a pregnant animal, the fetus is considered fit to receive sanctity. And Rabbi Meir holds “grasp the first expression,” even though at first, when he said “it is a peace offering,” he did not intend it for its offspring.
tosafot:a12.1: It is a peace offering and its offspring a burnt offering, it is the offspring of a peace offering: For as soon as he said “it is a peace offering,” the sanctity of his mouth also takes effect on the fetus as on the mother (a parenthetical phrase here is garbled in the printed text). And even according to the one who holds that if he reserved it, it is reserved, he nevertheless cannot change it to another sanctity, for as soon as he consecrated the mother he intended that the same sanctity take effect through his words on the fetus, and he cannot change it from the mother’s sanctity unless he first mentioned the sanctity of the offspring. And Rashi explained: “Here it is not relevant to say ‘as they come into being’ or ‘in their mother’s womb,’ for when one says ‘as they come into being’ and not in their mother’s womb, that applies where he consecrated it and afterward it became pregnant, where he did not involve the fetus in any sanctity except through the sanctity of its mother that he consecrated; but where one consecrates a pregnant animal, the fetus is considered fit to receive sanctity.” Up to here [Rashi’s] wording. If so, regarding what was said above [in the mishna on 24b], “and if female, a peace offering,” which we established as a consecrated animal, one must say it speaks of where he consecrated it and afterward it became pregnant.
gershom:a13.1: MISHNA: One who says “the offspring of this is a burnt offering” and afterward said “its mother will be a peace offering,” his statement stands, since he first consecrated the offspring as a burnt offering. But if he said first “it is a peace offering” and afterward said “its offspring is a burnt offering,” it is the offspring of a peace offering, as the fetus is the thigh of its mother and is seized by its mother’s sanctity.
rashi:a13.1: Since it is impossible to call two designations simultaneously: As the mouth cannot say two things at once.
rashi:a13.2: His statement stands: For a person is held even to the end of his words, since at first, when he said “it is a peace offering,” he did not intend it for its offspring.
gershom:a14.1: And Rabbi Yosei says: If that was his intent at first, to say first “its offspring is a burnt offering and it is a peace offering,” and he wished to consecrate both thus — even though he erred and said first “it is a peace offering,” not deliberately — since he wished to consecrate both, and it is impossible for the mouth to call two designations at once without one preceding the other, even though he erred and said “it is a peace offering” first, since he did not intend so from the outset, his statement stands. But if, after he deliberately said first “this is a peace offering,” he reconsidered and afterward said “and its offspring is a burnt offering,” he has said nothing, [but it is the offspring of a peace offering].
rashi:a14.1: GEMARA: If he wishes he may achieve atonement with its offspring: For when we say that the offspring of a sin offering goes to its death, that applies where he consecrated it and afterward it became pregnant; but if he consecrated it while pregnant, the fetus is considered fit to receive sanctity in its own right through its mother, and it is like one who separates two sin offerings as a guarantee, who achieves atonement with whichever he wishes.
tosafot:a14.1: If he wishes he may achieve atonement with its offspring: For when we say (above, Temurah 21b) that the offspring of a sin offering goes to its death, that applies where he consecrated it and afterward it became pregnant; but if he consecrated it while pregnant, the fetus is considered fit to receive sanctity in its own right and not by force of its mother, and it is like one who separates [two] sin offerings as a guarantee, who achieves atonement with whichever he wishes. Rashi’s wording.
rashi:a15.1: If he reserved it: The offspring, saying: Its offspring is non-sacred and it is a sin offering, it is reserved and is non-sacred. And since, if he wished, it would not be sanctified, evidently it is not the thigh of its mother; so when he does not reserve it, it is also not the thigh of its mother, and it is sanctified on its own account and not on account of its mother, and it is not like the offspring of a sin offering.
tosafot:a15.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that if he reserved the offspring, saying “its offspring is non-sacred and it is a sin offering,” it is reserved and is non-sacred: And since, if he wished, it would not be sanctified, evidently it is not the thigh of its mother; so when he does not reserve it, it is also not the thigh of its mother, and it is sanctified on its own account and not on account of its mother, and it is not the offspring of a sin offering. Rashi’s wording.
gershom:a15.1: GEMARA: What is the reason? He holds: if he reserved it, it is reserved. For if he achieved atonement with the [mother] animal and her offspring remained, it is reserved, and it is not considered like the offspring of a sin offering, which dies. Rather, since it was pregnant before he consecrated it, it is like one who consecrated the fetus alone and its mother alone, as the fetus is not the thigh of its mother; rather, it is reserved, so that it does not die but grazes, for its law is like one who separates two sin offerings as a guarantee, where the second grazes.
rashi:a17.1: It is the offspring of a peace offering: Evidently, since it calls it “the offspring of a peace offering,” the sanctity comes down to it by force of its mother and not on its own account; and with a sin offering too it is called the offspring of a sin offering and goes to its death. For if it enters your mind that if he reserved it, it is reserved, so that it is considered an animal in its own right, and when he did not reserve it, it is sanctified on its own account, it should have taught: “The offspring itself is a peace offering.”
tosafot:a17.1: It is the offspring of a peace offering: Evidently it calls it the offspring of a peace offering because the sanctity comes down to it by force of its mother and not on its own account; for with a sin offering too it is called the offspring of a sin offering and goes to its death.
tosafot:a17.2: For if it enters your mind that if he reserved it, it is reserved: So that it is considered an animal in its own right, and when he did not reserve it, it is sanctified on its own account, it should have taught: “The offspring itself is a peace offering.” Rashi’s wording.
gershom:a16.1: And if it is so that if he reserved it, it is reserved, why do they call it “the offspring of a peace offering,” that is, sanctified through its mother? It should have said “it is a peace offering,” that is, sanctified on its own account. Rather, since it says “it is the offspring of a peace offering,” learn from it that the fetus is the thigh of its mother, and if he reserved it, it is not reserved.
rashi:a18.1: Apart from this one: Do not raise a difficulty from that, for it is an erroneous reading, as we teach: The offspring, it is a peace offering.
gershom:a17.1: Rav Tavla said to him: Apart from this one, which the tanna taught, etc. And at any rate, it is not difficult: “If she was pregnant, she acquired for him” a bill of manumission, and it is like one who emancipates half of his slave, who acquires [freedom for] half [of himself as] a freeman. And here too, when he said to her “your child is a freeman,” it became as though he transferred to her the freedom of one of her limbs, and the bill and the hand of the offspring come at once, as its mother has authority of her own to receive its bill for it. And one cannot say “what a maidservant acquires, her master acquires,” since there is some freedom in her. But if you say, etc.: can she acquire for it, to receive its bill?
rashi:a19.1: She acquired for him: And the offspring goes out to freedom.
rashi:b1.1: One who emancipates half of his slave: He acquired [freedom for] half [of himself], and half of him is a freeman. And even though he did not emancipate all of him, he has a hand to receive his bill, as his bill and his hand come at once.
rashi:b2.1: But if you say that if he reserved it, it is reserved: If he freed the mother and reserved the offspring, it is reserved for his service; evidently they are two bodies. Why did she acquire for it? It is like a slave who receives a bill of manumission for his fellow from the hand of his own master, where both are slaves of one man, and his fellow is not freed, for the master has not released the bill of manumission from his hand: since he gave it to his slave, it is as though he gave it into his own possession.
rashi:b2.2: As it is taught: It appears, etc., from the hand of his fellow’s master, who is not his own master: For with regard to that man, this slave, the agent to receive the bill, has a hand, since he is not his master.
gershom:b1.1: And isn’t it taught: It appears that a slave acquires his fellow’s bill [of manumission] from the hand of his fellow’s master: For since he is not the slave of the one giving the bill, he can therefore receive it from him and acquire it for his fellow; but not from the hand of his own master on behalf of his fellow, if both belonged to one master, because the hand of a slave is like the hand of his master, as what a slave acquires his master acquires. And if you say that if he reserved it, it is reserved, and a fetus is not the thigh of its mother, then it is not as though he transferred to her one of her limbs; so why did she acquire for it? Rather, since it says “if she was pregnant, she acquired for him,” learn from it that a fetus is the thigh of its mother, and it is difficult for Rabbi Yoḥanan.
rashi:b3.1: The offspring is like her: Freed.
rashi:b3.2: His statement stands: And the offspring is a slave.
gershom:b2.1: Because it is stated: “The woman and her children”: That is, for the offspring follows the woman and is like her.
rashi:b4.1: What is the derivation of the verse for the Rabbis: The verse implies rather [a ruling] in accordance with Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, that the offspring follow the mother.
gershom:b3.1: What is the derivation for the Rabbis: That is, what proof is the verse for the Rabbis? On the contrary, it is difficult for them; rather, it supports Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
rashi:b5.1: It is not reserved: Rather, it is the thigh of its mother, and therefore it goes out to freedom like her.
rashi:b6.1: And here this is the reason: Of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: that the verse revealed it explicitly, and not because it is the thigh of its mother; rather, it is a decree of the verse with regard to a maidservant.
rashi:b7.1: One who slaughters a sin offering: It now enters our mind that he consecrated it while pregnant.
gershom:b4.1: What, is it not a dispute of tanna’im, etc.: Since they found it alive.
gershom:b5.1: It is eaten only by males of the priesthood, etc.: That is, it has the full law of a sin offering.
rashi:b9.1: What, is it not that they disagree about this: That the first tanna, who gives it the status of a sin offering, holds that if he reserved it, it is reserved; and since it is considered an animal in its own right, even when he did not reserve it, sanctity takes effect on it in the womb. [Rashi reads the first tanna’s view the other way round from our printed text.]
rashi:b9.2: And the later tanna: Who gives it the status of non-sacred, holds that if he reserved it, it is not reserved; it is not considered an animal in its own right but is the thigh of its mother, and it is sanctified on account of its mother like other offspring of consecrated animals, and that sanctity does not come down upon it until the time of birth, as he holds that the offspring of consecrated animals are sanctified as they come into being and not before.
tosafot:b9.1:
In brief: [On Rashi’s reading] the first tanna holds that if he reserved it, it is reserved: since he could make the offspring non-sacred, it is an animal in its own right, so when he consecrates the mother as a sin offering, his words also sanctify the offspring, and it is not eaten [by everyone]. The later tanna holds it is not reserved: it is like its mother’s thigh and is sanctified only through her, as they come into being; a four-month fetus found alive never came into being, so it is eaten by everyone.

Our teacher the RaMaR asked: in the mishna (“it is a peace offering and its offspring a burnt offering, it is the offspring of a peace offering”), Rashi explained that where one consecrated a pregnant animal the offspring is sanctified through its mother at once, and the Gemara reads that mishna as holding that what is reserved is not reserved, yet he cannot change the offspring. If, as here, it is non-sacred on that view, why can he not consecrate it as a burnt offering? He answered: the mother’s sanctity fixes it so that he cannot give it another sanctity, and it takes effect on it as soon as it is born; but until birth it is non-sacred, and if he slaughtered the mother meanwhile, it is eaten by everyone. The earlier mishna’s “if female, a peace offering” (24b), set in a consecrated animal, speaks where he consecrated it and afterward it became pregnant; one must distinguish the two cases.

Some books read the reverse (the first tanna: not reserved; the later: reserved, so the offspring is non-sacred). That cannot stand: even if the mother’s sanctity does not reach the offspring, his own words should, as the mishna teaches. Also, in the first chapter (Temurah 10a) these two baraitot are cited for the dispute of bar Padda and Rabbi Yoḥanan, so the one that says it is not eaten must follow Rabbi Yoḥanan, who holds it is reserved. Rather, Rashi’s reading is the correct one.

gershom:b6.1: What, is it not that they disagree about this: That the first tanna holds that if he reserved it, it is not reserved, but it is the thigh of its mother and its law is like its mother’s; and the later tanna holds that if he reserved the fetus [it is reserved], so that if he wished to consecrate it on its own for another offering he could, and it is not the thigh of its mother, and its law is not like its mother’s. And some say the reverse: that the first tanna holds that if he reserved it, it is reserved, as he can consecrate it on its own as a sin offering, and therefore its law is like a sin offering; and the other tanna holds that if he reserved it, it is not reserved.
rashi:b10.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan could say to you that everyone: If we are dealing with one who consecrated it while pregnant, certainly if he reserved it, it is reserved, and when he did not reserve it, the offspring is sanctified as a full sin offering. But where he consecrated it and afterward it became pregnant they disagree, and this is what they disagree about: one Sage holds as they come into being, and one Sage holds in their mother’s womb.
rashi:b11.1: Here, where he consecrated it and afterward it became pregnant, etc.: And everyone holds they are sanctified as they come into being and not in their mother’s womb. And the one that teaches that it is sanctified as a sin offering is where it became pregnant and afterward he consecrated it, as everyone holds that if he reserved it, it is reserved, and it is considered fit to be sanctified in its own right; and these tanna’im do not disagree at all.
gershom:b7.1: And if you wish, say: They are not difficult. The one that gives it the law of its mother speaks where it became pregnant and afterward he consecrated it: since he could have consecrated the fetus alone and its mother alone, it has the law of a sin offering. And the other tanna, who does not give it the law of a sin offering, speaks where he consecrated it and afterward it became pregnant: since at the time of consecration there was no fetus that he could consecrate, its law is therefore not like its mother’s.
rashi:b13.1: Rava objects to this: To that which we raised against Rabbi Yoḥanan from “if she was pregnant, she acquired for him,” and established it as a refutation.
rashi:b13.2: Who tells us that Rabbi Yoḥanan’s reason is because if he reserved it, it is reserved: So that it should be a refutation?
rashi:b13.3: Perhaps Rabbi Yoḥanan’s reason: Is that even though it is sanctified by force of its mother, it does not go to its death, because a person achieves atonement with the enhancement of consecrated property; and the offspring of a sin offering goes to its death where he did not wish to achieve atonement with it but with its mother.
gershom:b8.1: Perhaps this is the reason of Rabbi Yoḥanan, who said: If he wishes he achieves atonement with it, if he wishes he achieves atonement with its offspring: because a person achieves atonement with the enhancement of consecrated property, which is the offspring.
rashi:b14.1: Rav Hamnuna said to him: You cannot say that Rabbi Yoḥanan’s reason is not because if he reserved it, it is reserved; it is certainly for that reason, as Rabbi Elazar, who objected to Rabbi Yoḥanan above from “it is a peace offering and its offspring a burnt offering, it is the offspring of a peace offering,”
rashi:b14.2: was Rabbi Yoḥanan’s student and sat before him: And he objected to him, and Rabbi Yoḥanan did not answer him with this answer, to say to him: I hold that it is sanctified by force of its mother and not on its own account, and my reason is that a person achieves atonement with the enhancement of consecrated property.
tosafot:b14.1: And you say Rabbi Yoḥanan’s reason is because he holds a person achieves atonement with the enhancement of consecrated property: This is puzzling, as here it implies that Rabbi Yoḥanan holds a person does not achieve atonement with the enhancement of consecrated property; yet in the last chapter of Keritot (27a) Rabbi Elazar asked Rabbi Yoḥanan whether one achieves atonement with the enhancement of consecrated property or not, and he said to him: How many [years] has this one grown up among us, and he still does not know whether one achieves atonement with the enhancement of consecrated property or not! Evidently he holds that one does. One must distinguish between the enhancement of consecrated property in a thanks offering and the enhancement of consecrated property in a sin offering, and here it is a sin offering.
gershom:b9.1: Rav Hamnuna said to him: Rabbi Elazar was a student of Rabbi Yoḥanan and sat before him, and he raised an objection to him from “it is a peace offering and its offspring a burnt offering” (a garbled parenthetical follows in the printed text).
gershom:b10.1: And he did not answer him with this answer: Rather, Rav Tavla said to him: Apart from this one, etc.
gershom:b11.1: And you say, etc.: Rather, since he did not answer him so, learn from it that Rabbi Yoḥanan’s reason is because if he reserved it, it is reserved.
rashi:b15.1: Can one change his mind anytime that he wants: [Said] in astonishment.
rashi:b16.1: Within the time required for speaking: The time of a teacher’s greeting to a student; and some say, of a student to a teacher (Bava Kamma 73b).
tosafot:b16.1: It is necessary only where he said it within the time required for speaking: Meaning, the time of a student’s greeting to a teacher, “Peace be upon you, my teacher”; for that which we hold (Bava Batra 120b), that within the time required for speaking is like speaking, that is the time of a teacher’s greeting to a student.
rashi:b17.1: MISHNA: This is the substitute of a burnt offering: For Rabbi Meir holds “grasp the first expression.”
gershom:b12.1: MISHNA: This is the substitute of a burnt offering and the substitute of a peace offering; this is the substitute of a burnt offering, the statement of Rabbi Meir: For he holds “grasp the first expression.”
rashi:b18.1: His statement stands: And half of it is the substitute of a burnt offering and half the substitute of a peace offering, and it grazes until it becomes blemished and is sold, and with the money of half of it he brings [an offering for] the substitute of a burnt offering, and with the money of half [an offering for] the substitute of a peace offering. And we are dealing here with a case where a burnt offering and a peace offering were before him when he substituted this one for them.
gershom:b13.1: Rabbi Yosei says: If that was his intent at first, that it be the substitute of both, even though he did not say “this is the substitute of a burnt offering and a peace offering” but said “this is the substitute of a burnt offering (and the substitute of a peace offering) [and a peace offering]” [the printed text corrects itself here and the clause is unclear], since it is impossible, etc., his statement stands; and it is sold, and with half its money he brings the substitute of a burnt offering and with half the substitute of a peace offering.
gershom:b14.1: If after he said “the substitute of a burnt offering” he afterward reconsidered and said, etc.: It is the substitute of a burnt offering only. Both are sanctified, and it is sold, and with the money of half of it he brings the substitute of a burnt offering and with the money of half the substitute of a peace offering. [So the printed text.]
